core_concepts: IN LATE 2012, I was sitting in an old apartment just a few blocks from Istanbul’s most famous street, Istiklal Caddesi
There were seven of us, and I was the only one who hadn’t, at some point, smoked at least one pack of cigarettes per day
What was truly fascinating was that half of the people in the room had managed to quit smoking
“It frees you from the mental burden of smoking,” he said
I had never tried a cigarette, but I took a look at the book afterward out of curiosity
■ You think you are quitting something, but you’re not quitting anything because cigarettes do nothing for you
■ You think smoking is something you need to do to be social, but it’s not
■ You think smoking is about relieving stress, but it’s not
Over and over, he repeats these phrases and others like them
By the time you get to the end of the book, smoking seems like the most ridiculous thing in the world to do
mechanisms_or_explanations: I asked one of the Turks how he got started
Mike had been smoke-free for a few years at that point, and he swore up and down that he broke the habit because of a book called Allen Carr’s Easy Way to Stop Smoking
He says things like: ■ You think you are quitting something, but you’re not quitting anything because cigarettes do nothing for you
And if you no longer expect smoking to bring you any benefits, you have no reason to smoke

I often have a craving that goes something like this: “I want to eat tacos.” If you were to ask me why I want to eat tacos, I wouldn’t say, “Because I need food to survive.” But the truth is, somewhere deep down, I am
The underlying motive is to obtain food and water even if my specific craving is for a taco
Prediction: If I touch it I’ll get burned, so I should avoid touching it
Prediction: If I step on the gas, I’ll make it safely through the intersection and get closer to my destination, so I should step on the gas
This all happens in an instant, but it plays a crucial role in your habits because every action is preceded by a prediction
All day long, you are making your best guess of how to act given what you’ve just seen and what has worked for you in the past
Put another way, our behavior is heavily dependent on how we interpret the events that happen to us, not necessarily the objective reality of the events themselves
These predictions lead to feelings, which is how we typically describe a craving—a feeling, a desire, an urge
